title: Olumo Rock, Abeokuta: A Rock That Sheltered a People
excerpt: Olumo Rock rises about 137 metres above sea level in Abeokuta. Here is the history behind it and what to think about before you go.

children.text: Olumo Rock stands in Abeokuta, the capital of Ogun State in south-western Nigeria. It rises about 137 metres (449 feet) above sea level and is one of the best-known landmarks in the region.
A natural fortress

In the 19th century, the rock served the Egba people as a natural fortress during periods of inter-tribal warfare. It offered shelter and a high lookout from which approaching enemies could be seen. Abeokuta itself grew as settlers spread out from this area, and the name of the city is commonly translated from Yoruba as “under the rock”.
A place of cultural importance

Olumo is also a spiritual landmark. Its patron spirit is venerated in Yoruba religion, and the Egba still hold the rock in high esteem. Caves, rock shelters and shrine areas around the site give visitors a sense of how the rock has been used and respected over time.
Tips for your visit
Wear shoes with good grip. Paths around natural rock can be uneven.
Bring water and sun protection, and plan for time outdoors.
Ask your guide before photographing shrines or religious spaces, and respect any rules at those spots.
Confirm opening times and entry arrangements before you travel, as these can change.

title: Zuma Rock: The Monolith at the Gateway to Abuja
excerpt: Zuma Rock is a huge granite-type monolith beside the Abuja–Kaduna road. Learn what it is, why it matters and how to plan a visit.

children.text: Zuma Rock is a massive monolith near Madalla in Suleja Local Government Area, Niger State, beside the main Abuja–Kaduna road. Although many people assume it is in the Federal Capital Territory, it lies just across the boundary in Niger State.
What it is

Zuma Rock is an inselberg formed from an igneous intrusion of gabbro and granodiorite, and it dates to the Precambrian. It rises roughly 725 metres (2,379 feet) above sea level, with about 300 metres of prominence above the surrounding land. It is sometimes called the “Gateway to Abuja” from Suleja.
Culture and folklore

The rock has long been significant to local communities. The Gbagyi are recorded as having used it as a defensive retreat during inter-tribal wars, and local traditions describe a guardian deity and many stories about the rock. It also appears on the Nigerian 100-naira banknote.
Planning your visit
It is best viewed in clear weather. Haze and cloud can hide its full shape.
Leave time to stop along the road for photographs and take care near traffic.
Confirm access arrangements and any entry rules before you go.

title: Inside Nike Art Gallery in Lekki: What to Expect
excerpt: Nike Art Gallery in Lekki is a five-storey space filled with Nigerian art. Here is what makes it a favourite stop for visitors to Lagos.

children.text: Nike Art Gallery in Lekki, Lagos, is owned by the artist and cultural entrepreneur Nike Davies-Okundaye. It is housed in a five-storey building and is reported to hold around 8,000 artworks, making it one of the largest galleries of its kind in West Africa.
What you will see
The collection includes work by many Nigerian artists, across paintings, textiles and sculpture, displayed floor by floor. The gallery also has branches in Abuja, Oshogbo and Ogidi.
Tips for your visit
Allow plenty of time. With so many pieces across several floors, a rushed visit misses a lot.
Ask before photographing artworks, and ask staff about purchases directly.
Confirm opening hours before you go.
